Good morning! That clock you are looking at is my favorite thing on the stall.
It is beautiful. Look at the patina on the wood. How old is it?
About a hundred years. It belonged to a family who lived in Bath. It was an heirloom.
Really? So why did they sell it?
The grandson, who lives in Canada now, had no space for it. He was very sad to let it go.
I understand. Some things have a sentimental value that money cannot pay. How much is it?
Eighty pounds. But it is the clock that everybody stops to look at.
In Brazil we always haggle a little at a market. Would you take sixty?

My name is Greta, and I live in Hamburg. Every Sunday I go to the flea market, which is next to the river. Three years ago I saw an old brown suitcase, which was covered with hotel labels from the nineteen fifties: Rome, Lisbon, Cairo. The man who was selling it wanted forty euros. We haggled for ten minutes, which is completely normal at a German flea market, and I paid twenty-five. At home I opened it and found a name inside the lid: Hannelore Weiss. I was curious, so I searched online, and I found a woman whose grandmother had that name. She lived in a small town near Bremen. I wrote to her, and she cried on the phone. The suitcase was the one that her grandmother took on her honeymoon. I gave it back to her. I did not ask for the twenty-five euros. Some things have a value that you cannot put on a price tag.

I am Tom, and I restore old furniture in a small workshop in York, which used to be a bakery. People think my job is about wood and glue, but really it is about stories. A few years ago, a lady brought me a writing desk that she had bought at an auction. One of the drawers, which had been stuck for decades, would not open. When I finally got it open, I found a letter. It was from a young soldier who was writing to his mother in nineteen sixteen. He told her not to worry, and he asked her to save him some of her apple cake. We never found out if he came home. The lady, whose own grandfather had been a soldier, decided not to sell the desk. She framed the letter and put it on the wall, right above the desk. That desk was worth about two hundred pounds. Now it is worth its weight in gold.
